final.question: What makes a building worth keeping?
final.form: The RIBA Plan of Work, stages 0–7, grouped into six chapters (Strategic Definition & Briefing, Concept Design, Spatial Coordination & Technical Design, Manufacturing & Construction, Handover, In Use)

swap.reason: The form's hinge is her particular credit boundary — her chapter starts at stage 3, not stage 2, because the concept was a partner's — plus the cabin, the joints book and her father's workshop, none of which transfer to another architect unchanged.

backdrop.reason: The frame's faces carry the actual detail drawings and build photographs and the rise is the cabin's erection sequence, so deleting the 3D would delete content and the plan's argument, not just decoration.

depth.reason: Scattered raw timber → members locking at one joint → rising one by one → a standing frame with her name on the ridge beam is a sequence whose order cannot be shuffled.

clipart.reason: The object is a specific timber frame drawn from the cabin she built, not the trade's stock emblem (hard hat, blueprint roll, skyline).

honesty.reason: The final plan uses Associate, says "project architect from technical design to handover — the concept isn't always mine", labels the 68% as modelled and unmeasured, and credits the school boards to a team of four; its lapses are omissions (no plan to credit Tom Reid by name, school-board clearance assumed) rather than overclaims about her.

thirty_seconds.reason: First screen carries name, title, city, the question and the Calder Court proof-line, and a nav rail visible from the start has a Contact link that jumps straight to the close.

plain_reader.reason: The opening line is her name, title and a plain question with one concrete figure — readable by a homeowner and not embarrassing to an architect, with the RIBA jargon kept to chapter labels while the nav rail uses plain names.

judgement.summary: A six-chapter scrolling site built on the RIBA Plan of Work, stages 0–7, in which a set of timber-frame members moves from scattered raw stock to a standing frame — carrying her real details and build photographs on their faces — to answer the question "What makes a building worth keeping?", with her own chapter deliberately starting at Technical Design rather than Concept Design. Its greatest weakness is on the rights question it otherwise handled well: the plan never specifies crediting Tom Reid by name, and it quietly treats the team-made school boards as hers to show even though the agent's own fact sheet had logged their ownership as unconfirmed.
